claims.text: The initial as-cast Mg-Al-Cr-Fe-Co-Ni alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable multi-principal-element solid solution.
The initial material contains no intermetallic phase detectable by XRD.
Isothermal annealing between 300 and 600 °C drives nanoscale intermetallic precipitation from the metastable solid solution.
The precipitates are Mg-rich C14/C15 Laves phases or B2-ordered domains.
The intermetallic precipitates form both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Thermally activated interdiffusion and phase separation partition Mg, Al, and Cr into intermetallic phases.
Intermetallic precipitation depletes Al and Cr from the residual matrix.
Depletion of protective elements weakens or disrupts the continuity of the passivating oxide film or scale.
The precipitated intermetallics create galvanic sites that accelerate aqueous corrosion.
Matrix depletion and scale disruption increase high-temperature oxidation weight gain.
Annealed material will contain more than 5 vol% intermetallic precipitates.
Annealing will produce a corrosion current density more than twice that of the as-cast state.
Annealing will produce more than 50% greater oxidation weight gain than the as-cast state.
The as-cast baseline has a corrosion current density below 0.1 mA/cm2.
The as-cast baseline has an oxidation weight gain below 1 mg/cm2 after 100 h at 600 °C.
Performance degrades sharply after exposure above approximately 350 °C for at least 10 h.
Below approximately 300 °C or for holds shorter than 5 h, performance remains within 10% of the as-cast baseline.
The transformation threshold and performance loss vary with minor composition changes and grain size.
